text: This capstone used every chapter that came before it. Chapter one is why Lesson twenty-nine didn't need to argue that hybrid architecture is normal -- Alderney's regulated claims workload is exactly the permanent, structural hybrid estate Chapter one described. Chapter two is the entire subject of Lesson thirty-one: Brennick Retail is a direct, illustrative consequence of ignoring its warning about blanket multi-cloud policy.

Chapter three is the backbone of Lesson thirty end to end -- the Kubernetes portability boundary and the multi-cloud Terraform module pattern are the exact tools that deployed one workload identically to AKS and EKS. Chapter four is why Lesson twenty-nine's identity design was a single conditional access policy spanning on-prem and cloud, rather than two separate access models. And Chapter five is why that lesson's network design used a private ExpressRoute circuit instead of a public internet path.

Chapter six is why Lesson twenty-nine's data classification step came first, before any infrastructure was designed -- data gravity and residency requirements are what decided raw data stays on-prem permanently. Chapter seven is the layer underneath Lesson thirty-one's entire case study -- Brennick's missing cost model is precisely the unified cross-cloud cost view this course built, and its absence is what let the real cost hide for three years.

Read together, the two labs and the case study teach the same discipline from both directions. Lessons twenty-nine and thirty show hybrid and multi-cloud done deliberately, with a specific requirement driving every decision. Lesson thirty-one shows what happens when the same tools get reached for by default, with no requirement and no cost model checking the result. These tools aren't good or bad in themselves -- they earn their cost only when a real requirement, not a slogan, is driving the design.

This course is complete, and it's one of four Expert Specialization courses in the Cloud Engineer to Cloud Architect path. These four build on the Advanced Specialization stage but not on each other, so they can be taken in any order from here: Advanced Platform Engineering, GitOps and CI/CD; AI Cloud Infrastructure, GPU Computing and MLOps; and Advanced Site Reliability Engineering, Disaster Recovery and Resilience.

Hybrid and Multi-Cloud Enterprise Architecture is done -- eight chapters covering fundamentals, strategy, portability, identity, networking, data, cost, and governance, proven on one regulated workload and one cautionary tale. From here, pick up any of the three remaining Expert Specialization courses, in whichever order makes the most sense for where you're headed next.
